Lightkeepers

Silvestr Petrovich Solovei was born in the far north of Snezhnaya more than five hundred years ago and belonged to an illustrious family whose emblem was a nightingale, a mark of their distinguished heritage. Members of his family had once served as spies, but were elevated to the gentry by the Belyi Tsar. And thus did Silvestr step into the royal palace, now mingling among the Fae dignitaries of the court. Since childhood, Silvestr had been friends with Avrelian, an orphan from Nod-Krai, the ideal heir to the Frostmoon Scions, whose mother had committed suicide when spies wanted to force her to return to the homeland. As a child, Avrelian often spoke of his dream of creating an Elysium on earth and railed against the gods and the rich. During Avrelian's lifetime, Silvestr never understood his friend's idea, and only after he had become the notorious thief Reed Miller and was executed for his crimes did Solovei understand the true meaning of these words and decide to save this dream.
Among the Belyi Tsar's court was a monk, Rotwang, exiled from Khaenri’ah for studying dark knowledge. One day, he glimpsed a pitch-black Elysium and was willing to do anything to achieve it. He knew the Archon had a daring plan to seize power capable of upending the world and becoming ruler of the sublunar world, but he believed the Belyi Tsar could have thought wider. When the Belyi Tsar sent Rotwang to Nod-Krai to retrieve the treasure hidden there, the monk decided to seize it for himself to achieve the pitch-black Elysium. Back in Snezhnaya, Rotwang allied with the Archpriestess of the Frostmoon Scions to use the ideal heir from their prophecy. Rotwang convinced Avrelian to take the Frostmoon Scions' sacred relic, the Sampo Mill, promising to create Elysium together.

After the death of his friend, Solovei traveled to Avrelian's homeland, Nod-Krai, where he met twin sisters from the Frostmoon Scions, Aila and Alia. According to prophecy, they were the chosen ones, destined to bear the ideal heir who would lead the Frostmoon Scions to Elysium. Alia understood that Rotwang and Lovia's plan could lead to the deaths of countless people, so she pretended to be Solovei's close friend and gained his trust. When Professor Rotwang built a heaven-reaching tower in Nod-Krai, named the Pillar of Embla, he intended to use the Sampo Mill to siphon the land's power and, through that tower, ascend to the "Elysium" he believed lay beyond the sky. Had his scheme succeeded, all of Nod-Krai — its soil and every living being upon it — would have become fuel for his ascent. Alia and Solovei did all they could to stop him, but at the time, they were too weak. When they reached the Pillar of Embla, Rotwang was one step away from his goal. Realizing there was no other choice, Alia cast herself into the Sampo Mill and, with her own body, ignited it with the purified blood of the Frostmoon Scions. Along with Alia, Solovei's former nightingale was also sucked in. Alia's sacrifice thwarted the Professor's plans and destroyed him for the first time.

When the Cataclysm struck Teyvat five hundred years ago, the Belyi Tsar's court could no longer mind the remote borderlands beyond the snowy plains. The horde of pitch-black beasts tore across the barren land, destroying all traces of past civilization. Countless souls lie buried within the ancient ruins, innumerable heroes faded where mists now stray. It was not until Silvestr arrived at the abandoned by the gods Nod-Krai. To combat the forces of the Abyss and the Wild Hunt, priestess Aila shared with Solovei, whom she saw as the hero meant to protect "Elysium," a sacred relic of the Frostmoon Scions left by Hyperborea, the Arrow of Terpikeraunas. It was capable of transforming the energy of the Light Realm and purifying the energy of the Void Realm (the Abyss). Borrowing the priestess's power, Solovei raised that first beam of light and, in the name of the moon, banished the darkness to those lightless ruins, burying it deep down alongside the nightmare-torn souls. Since Aila had the ability to see the future, she foresaw Rotwang's return from the impenetrable darkness, and Solovei decided to found an order that would meet the threat with Hyperborean technology. He named this order the Lightkeepers, in honor of the flame Aila had ignited, and he himself became the first Torchforger and the first Starshyna. A nightingale holding a burning wick in its beak became an insignia of the Lightkeepers. After Rotwang's first "death" at the Pillar of Embla, he returned as a being woven from the Abyss. Solovei and Aila were able to push the fiend and his followers back to Kipumaki Cliff and seal them there.

When the Cataclysm ended, the surviving Lightkeepers built a lighthouse and their own city, Piramida, on the mountaintop where Governor Trubetskoy's palace had once stood. The Arrow of Terpikeraunas became a foundation of Piramida. Solovei resolved to preserve the pure childhood dream of his friend, Avrelian, and was unafraid to defend it before the judgment of the new Archon, the Tsaritsa. The First Torchforger asked the Cryo Archon for autonomy for the borderlands, taking upon himself an oath of vigilance and sacrifice. And thus began the history of the "paradise" known as "Nod-Krai," and the Torchforger, bathed in the moon's eternal light, lit the everlasting flame and began his watch.

<color=#ffffffd9>"We shall part the snow-curtain of the sky, and blast the winter winds across the wasteland."</color>
<color=#ffffffd9>"We are the Lightkeepers, who shine the eternal light of hope into the endless snow-swept plains."</color>

The main foe of the Lightkeepers, whose ranks are now entirely composed of volunteers, is the Wild Hunt, a special manifestation of the Abyss that arose in Nod-Krai during the Cataclysm five hundred years ago. When one of the Five Sinners of Khaenri'ah, the
entered the reflection of the moon, a force tore him apart, but the Abyssal powers he had obtained, like a curse, preserved his life. Parts of Rerir's body found their way to Nod-Krai, and their corruption awakened the buried warriors of the ancient kingdom, who became the Wild Hunt. In northern Nod-Krai, the Wild Hunt gained special abilities under the influence of Professor Rotwang and his followers, and for five hundred years, the Lightkeepers have defended the borderlands from the Wild Hunt. Unlike the Marechaussee Hunters of the high seas, the Lightkeepers who patrolled the night did not possess any ancient techniques from a lost empire or prestigious titles and ranks. All they could rely on was weak flesh clad in silver armor, the swords and lamps in their hands, and an ancient oath passed down through generations. Their lit lantern dispelled the darkness, so the borderlanders believed that as long as the Lightkeepers' lanterns burned, evil spirits would not enter the dwellings of the living. To protect themselves from the Wild Hunt, the Lightkeepers installed Tideseal Stones capable of dispelling the aura of the Abyss and began using oath lanterns, through which they can track each other. The Lightkeepers' oath states: <color=#ffffffd9>"Our bones and blood we shall use as fuel, we shall make life greater than death."</color> This means that if the Lightkeepers find themselves at a great disadvantage, their first priority is to preserve life and ensure the long-term survival of humanity, not to save themselves. And although this principle is harsh on those who must sacrifice themselves, most warriors are willing to follow it.

Hundreds of years after the Lightkeepers were founded, the Wild Hunt once again attacked the borderlands. As the rallying horns echoed through the hills, warriors formed ranks at the high tower's foot, awaiting the order to march south to fulfill their ancient oath. But the Lightkeepers' Starshyna sat in silence, for the warriors of the Pale Star of Snezhnaya had already approached the city gates to the north. These special forces, loyal to Her Majesty, the Tsaritsa, obeyed no Harbinger and vowed to create a new, pure world under the white stars. And although the uninvited guests claimed to be reinforcements, Starshyna knew they had other reasons for coming here. But to yield now would mean ending the autonomy they had defended for centuries. And so began a new battle. When the warriors of the Pale Star arrived in the borderlands, they were forbidden to interfere in the battle. And although the request to attack was rejected, their Warrant Officer secretly made the decision. He could not stand by and watch as those pitch-black beasts devour the land, snatching away the lives of mothers and their children. And when the northern wind dispersed the foul miasma, just as the first light of dawn pierces the coal-black clouds, its glow once more cast down upon the cerulean earth below, Piramida greeted not a hero, but a criminal, and the children had risked all to save. Desertion, treason against the Tsaritsa, were grave crimes, but a new oath was meant to grant pardon. Upon a staircase built of bones, new warriors took up their watch, there to stand till the abyssal tides dried up.

Ten years ago, a great battle returned to Nod-Krai. The air was thick with the scent of blood, as if signaling the return of the great war by which the earth had been scorched. It was a tempest, the likes of which had not been seen for a century, poured down upon the earth like black-blood rain. Someone had to face this terror, lighting the way for the souls wandering through the boundless dark. A black-feathered flock of crows moved between the realms of light and shadow, led by one who stood against the light. His sword he silently raised, the face reflected in its sheen as sharp and unyielding as the blade itself. Onward pressed the oath-bound legion, though they knew they were as moths to a flame, marching onto that battlefield from which none would return. In the end, only Starshyna Sigurd remained with his dark blade. He knew that the corruption that had caused the Wild Hunt lurked in the depths of the forest and hoped to destroy it. He didn't notice that his body had already been torn asunder, and the warning bell he carried rang out hissing amidst the tearing of blood and black muck. As many years went by, a new addition was woven into the folklore of the land: whenever mournful bells toll, it is a sign that the one who swore to hunt down the Wild Hunt is approaching. After Starshyna Sigurd's disappearance, the Lightkeepers built an empty grave in his honor near the Barrowmoss Barrens. Though his life's spark has been extinguished, his unbending will has yet to fade, and those who swore to become hunters of the Wild Hunt continue his endless battle even today. The dark abyss's corrosion has seeped into his marrow, causing him to lose his way, but the desire to defend hearth and home will surely reignite, reawakening him to continue a bitter, eternal battle. Sigurd's spirit can be found on Lempo Isle, where he continues to protect people from the Wild Hunt. Artifacts he once carried can be found in places where he has been seen.

customize.text: Flins

There is a small isle in the central-southern region of Nod-Krai that has earned the name "Final Night Cemetery" on account of its lonesome, dismal air. Before becoming a graveyard, the island's lighthouse served many purposes, from guiding passing merchants and Lightkeeper fleets to reporting on the Wild Hunt's activity in the surrounding area. The lighthouse's flame was never once extinguished, becoming a symbol of hope and warmth, but the light of this historic outpost was snuffed out in a conflict against the Wild Hunt several decades ago. Ninety percent of the Ratniki stationed on the island perished in that battle, and the Starshyna was forced to send a distress signal, saving nearby merchant fleets and patrolling Lightkeeper ships. Otherwise, they would have been drawn into the battle without any understanding of the situation. But at the same time, this signal deprived the troops on the island of any chance of escape. The odds were stacked against them, and they would not have been able to hold out, but not a single one of them fled. Amidst the sludge-sullied tundra, now soaked in the blood of heroes, a young warrior knelt among the bodies of his fallen comrades. Bleeding to death, one of the Ratniki traced symbols on the stone slate with his own blood, praying to everyone who could hear, calling for salvation. At the cost of blood and souls, the phantom sleeping beneath this slab awoke from a long, deep sleep and answered his prayers. That ghostly blue wildfire of which ancient legends spoke would burn brightly anew on fresh fields of battle.

In Snezhnaya, there is a legend about Kyryll the Azure Flame: he was originally a blue flame that guided fallen souls across the icy plains, but during the transition of power from the Belyi Tsar to the Tsaritsa, he disappeared. Kyryll the Azure Flame, or as he is known in Nod-Krai, the Lantern Fae, is a noble Fae from Snezhnaya, named Kyryll Chudomirovich Flins. His family crest and surname remain in the register of Snezhnayan nobility, and he was once a member of the Belyi Tsar's royal court. But when the blue flames were completely replaced by the red flames of the Tsaritsa, Flins left Snezhnaya due to the divergence with the regime change. After traveling south by rail, passing through snowy plains, thriving cities, and deserted lands, Flins found himself on a small island beneath a lighthouse. There, Kyryll the Azure Flame found the perfect place to end his life. He chose stone slates, built an altar, and sealed himself with ancient rituals. But before he could sink into the impenetrable abyss, he was awakened by the prayers of a young warrior. The first light Flins saw upon awakening was the light of the Lightkeepers' eyes. And although he was unable to prevent the losses, he, along with the survivors, founded a cemetery on this island and decided to join the Ratniki to experience human life.

After joining the Lightkeepers, Flins continued to live on the Final Night Cemetery, guarding the peace of the warriors who fell there. To check on his well-being away from Piramida, Starshyna Nikita sometimes sends Ratniki to the island. One of the people who appears in the Final Night Cemetery is the young Lightkeeper, Illuga, to whom Flins often tells various stories about the reign of the Belyi Tsar and the Fae. And although Flins never tells the truth, and all his stories remain untold, it cannot be said that he lies. He once told Illuga a story about the "Tear of the North," a perfect, transparent blue gem, said to have been formed from the courage of Snezhnayan soldiers fighting in the northern territories, capable of protecting its bearer. One day, at a social event of the Belyi Tsar, a man bet a noble Fae that a dancer would become drunk without drinking five glasses. He won the bet, and the Fae gave him the "Tear of the North," which Flins later acquired. In fact, this Fae was Flins himself, who had received this gem from the Belyi Tsar. The man who received the gem from him wanted to resell it, but was unable to get a good price. The gem passed from hand to hand until it was finally purchased by the Fae. One day, while the Lightkeepers were on patrol, the Ratniki decided to play cards and offered Flins a game. He pretended he'd never played before, listened attentively to all the rules, and apologized for the slow pace of the game. The Ratniki were sure the newcomer would have to lose a few rounds, so they had no intention of going easy on him, but that evening, all their games dragged on forever, and no one could win. Only during a game with the warrior Olav did Flins suddenly play two unlucky cards and lose. Later, when he was alone with Nikita, the leader of the Lightkeepers, who knew of Flins's origins, Nikita asked him, "Which is harder, then? Winning at cards or pretending you can't win?" Flins then replied that both were easier than pretending to be an ordinary person.

customize.text: Illuga

Ten years ago, when a battle broke out between the Wild Hunt and the Lightkeepers, a young family with a son named Illuga was ambushed by monsters. The mother defended her son to the last breath, but both parents were killed. When the boy awoke, he was surrounded by black curtains that leaped and twisted like tongues of flame. He remembered his mother's words about not crying, lest the monsters, searching for signs of life, find him. Soon, the screams and cries died down, and the monsters retreated, taking everyone with them. The Lightkeepers, sent south by Starshyna Sigurd, came to the child's aid. Lightkeeper Nikita took the surviving Illuga to Piramida and raised him as his own son. After the death of Sigurd and almost all the Ratniki in that great battle, Nikita assumed the position of Starshyna and had to rebuild the squad practically from scratch. At first, Nikita taught Illuga combat skills, but later realized that this method was unsuitable for raising children. He placed the war orphans in separate quarters and assigned special caregivers. Even so, the Starshyna regretted not giving the boy a happy life, leaving him behind in Piramida. And when Illuga decided to join the Lightkeepers, Nikita refused to send him to the front lines and assigned him to the supply squad. Logistics work involves many varied tasks — organizing supplies, collating reports, delivering messages, the list goes on. Before long, he had visited every outpost the Lightkeepers kept, both large and small, and there wasn't a Lightkeeper in Nod-Krai who wasn't familiar with this enthusiastic young man. He treated everyone like family, showing attentiveness and care. After a year in the supply squad, Illuga received orders to join the investigation squad, and his comrades believed the young man would lead them to a bright future.

Three years ago, Illuga's squad set out on an investigation mission near Kipumaki Cliff, where the First Torchforger and the Moochanter had imprisoned Professor Rotwang and his followers. An anomaly in the ancient ruins triggered the Wild Hunt, which swept across the northern lands of Nod-Krai. Illuga's squad was the first to notice the anomaly and set up camp on the rock for the night, but was awakened by the sounds of a struggle. Everything around was shrouded in a strange fog, from which intermittent human voices could be heard. They seemed familiar, yet unrecognizable. And within the fog, it turned out that the squad members were killing each other. Squad leader Ollson ordered a retreat, remaining behind to cover their retreat. Of the entire squad, only Illuga managed to escape and save his wounded and unconscious comrade. Illuga hurried to report the situation to the Starshyna, but when they returned with reinforcements, no one remained alive, and the Wild Hunt, pouring from Kipumaki Cliff, had spread to its foothills. Although Illuga did not flee the battlefield in fear, he was forced to leave the wounded behind to bring reinforcements. From that strange fog, he heard familiar, fragmented voices, seemingly mocking his cowardice. Illuga began to doubt his decision and asked Flins what was more unforgivable for a Lightkeeper: recklessness or cowardice. Flins replied, <color=#ffffffd9>"I'm afraid the premise of your question is misguided. To join the Lightkeepers is itself a testament to courage. And as a steadfast, upright Lightkeeper — what reason would you have to doubt your choices derive from a sense of justice?"</color> After this, Illuga submitted his request to assume command of the Nightmare Orioles investigation squad.

During a perilous mission, Illuga became separated from his squad and was lost in the endless expanse of a dark forest — an illusion created by the Wild Hunt — but he saw a faint glimmer that guided him out of the forest. Only when the moonlight pierced the mist did he see the light's source — a bird as translucent as crystal, radiant and pure. From then on, the nightingale often traveled by his side, helping him deal with countless problems, and wherever he was stationed, Illuga would always leave a place for it by his door. The bird, Aedon, once belonged to the first Torchforger and managed to escape from the Sampo Mill, where it had been drawn along with Alia of the Frostmoon Scions. Illuga later arrived at the Pillar of Embla to retrieve from Alia one of the sacred relics that held back the corruption of the Abyss and helped defeat Rotwang for the third and final time.

After that battle, Starshyna Nikita forbade the Lightkeepers from approaching Kipumaki Cliff. Three years later, when the seals of the Torchforger and the Moonchanter weakened, the professor's followers, along with Rotwang, broke free. Illuga's squad once again set out for the cliff to retrieve the Spiralblade, one of the three Lightkeepers' relics used by the Torchforger to seal demons. One of Rotwang's followers, who had become the Scourge of Endless Decay, the one behind the destruction of the Nightmare Orioles three years ago, began to provoke the squad again. After it recalled the deaths of Illuga's parents and his squad, the commander decided to confront the monster alone, ensuring no one else would suffer for his sake. Illuga's squad did not stand by and came to their commander's aid, destroying the Scourge of Endless Decay and acquiring the Spiralblade. When the Lightkeepers assembled their ultimate weapon, the Arrow of Terpikeraunas, they were able to destroy Rotwang and his followers for the third time, as the Moonchanter foretold.
